cells.tense: You are leaving something behind and your hands are steady while you do it.
cells.ask: Put the one thing you're leaving into a sentence, and name who you'd want beside you when you say it.
cells.core:
Something you were part of has run its course, and you're holding the whole of it without flinching. That isn't coldness. You can remember what it gave you and what it asked, and you can still stand in the middle of it and say what's true about it out loud.

The people who built it with you can feel you're not at war with it. That steadiness is what keeps the leaving clean instead of a wreck. It doesn't need deciding again every morning. Put the thing you're leaving into one sentence, and name who you'd want beside you when you say it. Then let that be the whole of it.

cells.tense: You are rehearsing your exit long before the ground has stopped holding under you.
cells.ask: Stay one more week without deciding. When you catch yourself rehearsing the ending, write down what you'd be walking toward — no plan, just the name.
cells.core:
The conversations, the reasoning, the version you'll tell people — it's all running ahead of where you actually stand. It feels like preparation, and some of it is. But you're spending today on a tomorrow that hasn't arrived, and the people still in the room with you can tell you've gone somewhere else.

What you'd leave can't be sorted from five feet away. Rehearsing is how you try to make the ground stop moving. Stay one more week without deciding. Each time you catch yourself writing the ending, write down instead what you'd be walking toward. Not a plan. Just the name. The staying is the work.

cells.tense: The signs have been coming for a while, and you're still standing in the doorway calling it undecided.
cells.ask: Say one plain sentence to someone about what you've stopped pretending is fine. Not what you'll do next — just that sentence.
cells.core:
The signs have been coming for a while — small ones, then not small — and underneath all of that sits something you keep letting sit. Saying it would mean losing a way of being, so you stay where the answer is still technically open.

It isn't open. You've been pulling on both ends of a rope with only one end left, and that takes energy you'd want for whatever comes after. You don't have to move anything today. You only have to stop protecting the uncertainty. Say one plain sentence to someone about what you've stopped pretending is fine, and see what the saying does.
cells.sheetLine: The ending may be true. You're the last one calling it undecided.

cells.tense: Something is already changing in how you spend your days, and you're calling it nothing.
cells.ask: Next time someone asks about that part of your life, say what you've actually been doing instead of saying it's fine.
cells.core:
You're already letting go of something, and the letting go is going well enough that you could almost miss it. Knowing what you're part of and what you're not, saying so plainly, showing up where you still want to — you can hold that, and the contact stays clean because nothing's being forced.

Right now, less of certain conversations, less reaching out, more time in things you'd rather not explain. It doesn't feel like leaving. It feels like the volume going down on its own, and you've been letting it look that way. But you're the one choosing it — small choices, made smoothly enough to pass as nothing. People have started asking. You say you're fine, and you are, you're just not saying what's happening. Say the real thing to one person who asks.
